sentences.text: The holotype, which is the specific specimen used to define the species, consists of partial skull bones measuring roughly 201 mm in length and 115 mm in width. Scientists estimate the full skull reached about 1.35 meters based on related skeletal remains. These bones show unique traits like two replacement teeth per socket and a sculptured secondary palate.

The animal possessed elongated neural spines on its vertebrae that formed a ridge or sail on its back. It also had large, robust forelimbs and relatively short hindlimbs, features common to spinosaurids.

Oxalaia quilombensis holds the record for the largest carnivorous dinosaur discovered in Brazil. It is also the biggest known theropod from the country, surpassing Pycnonemosaurus which was estimated at 8.9 meters long.
Fossils were recovered in 1999 from the Laje do Coringa locality on Cajual Island within the Alcântara Formation. The species was formally described in 2011 by Alexander Kellner and his colleagues.

Oxalaia lived in a tropical, heavily forested habitat surrounded by an arid landscape. As a spinosaurid, it likely spent most of its time near or in water to avoid direct competition with other large predators.

Fossil evidence suggests spinosaurids like Oxalaia also preyed on small dinosaurs and pterosaurs. Unlike its Early Cretaceous relatives Suchomimus and Cristatusaurus, Oxalaia lacked serrations on its teeth.
Tall neural spines on Oxalaia's tail vertebrae likely aided in swimming, similar to modern crocodilians. These high neural spines on the tail may have helped it swim like modern crocodiles.

Kellner and colleagues differentiated Oxalaia from other spinosaurids based on distinguishing craniodental features, including a sculptured palatal part of the premaxillae and two replacement teeth per position. These distinct features, such as the highly sculpted secondary palate, were not seen in other spinosaurids or theropods.

It is debated whether Oxalaia is a distinct genus or a junior synonym of Spinosaurus. In 2020, Robert Smyth and colleagues argued that the distinguishing features of Oxalaia quilombensis were insufficient for a separate taxon and were instead a result of individual variation. It is also debated whether Oxalaia is a modern synonym of the African genus Spinosaurus.
